1:
The register opens with a title, and the witnesses read its very first phrase as a confession of a nation's fall: these are the children of the province that went up out of the captivity. The reformed John Gill, following Jarchi, takes the province to be Judea itself, once a flourishing kingdom now reduced to a mere province of the Median and Persian empire, though he notes that Aben Ezra referred it rather to Babylon, where the exiles had been born or long dwelt. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke decides for Judea, since the same land is so styled elsewhere (Ezra 5:8), and since the verse itself sets the province over against Babylon, whither its children had been carried; behold, he says, the goodness and the severity of God. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley strikes the same note, that the historian calls Judah a province emphatically, to remind himself and his brethren of the sad change their sins had wrought, from an illustrious and independent kingdom to an obscure and servile dependency, first under the Chaldeans and now under the Persians.

The grammatical-historical witnesses supply the document's frame. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the title governs the whole list that follows, the men of the people of Israel who returned to Jerusalem and Judah under Zerubbabel, Joshua, and their fellow-leaders; the same register, they note, Nehemiah afterward found and incorporated into his own book (Nehemiah 7:6). Charles Ellicott traces the words closely: the people came from the captivity, now almost a proper name, the children of the captivity, and became children of the province, the Judaean province of Persia; and every one came to his city, so far, he adds, as his city was known.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology of the notice. That an account was kept in writing of the families who came up, he says, was for their honour, a recompence for the faith and courage that carried them home, and a spur to others; those that honour God he will honour, and the names of all true Israelites who accept deliverance by Christ are written in a more sacred record, the Lamb's book of life. Yet he does not miss the humbling truth in the word province: see how sin debases a nation, which righteousness would exalt. Made servants now, as the patriarchs were sojourners in a land promised them, they were being reminded of the better country, the heavenly one (Heb. 11:16), a kingdom that cannot be moved into a province. So the witnesses make this opening verse at once a record of shame and a token of hope, the roll of a humbled people whom God was bringing back to their own cities.
2:
The list of the returning host is headed by its leaders, the eleven named with Zerubbabel: Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. The reformed John Gill identifies the first of them, Jeshua, as Joshua the high priest, the son of Josedech, and then opens a question that would divide the witnesses. Dr. Lightfoot, he reports, held that this Nehemiah is the very man whose book bears the name, that Mordecai is Esther's kinsman, and that Seraiah, elsewhere called Azariah, is Ezra himself; but Gill judges with others that they are rather different men of the same names, since the famous Nehemiah came to Jerusalem only in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, and Mordecai was then raising Esther in Shushan.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry treats the leaders as the new Moses and Aaron of the people, Zerubbabel their chief prince and Jeshua their chief priest; and of the disputed names he takes the gentler view, that Nehemiah and Mordecai were probably the same famous men, who came now and afterward returned to court for their country's service. The two readings stand side by side, the one keeping the great names distinct from their earlier bearers, the other allowing one man to appear at more than one point of the history.

The grammatical-historical witnesses turn to the shape of the roll. Keil and Delitzsch set the Ezra text beside its twin, noting how the names and numbers vary between this register and the parallel in Nehemiah 7:8. Charles Ellicott observes that the leaders, perhaps meant to represent the twelve tribes, are given here by twelve names, save that one, Nahamani, has dropped out, while three others appear in slightly altered forms. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens the view to three witnesses, for the catalogue is preserved thrice, here, in Nehemiah, and in the apocryphal Esdras, and the copies correct one another; though the grand total agrees at forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty, the particulars fall short, and he reports Alting's reconciliation, that the surplus names of the one book, added to the other, bring both to the same sum. Wesley closes with the plainest account of the divergence, that several names were given to the same persons, and that many changes befell the families between Ezra's first making of the catalogue and its renewal so many years after. So the witnesses read the verse both as an honour-roll of the leaders and as the head of a document whose every later line they will weigh against its parallel.
3:
With the children of Parosh, two thousand a hundred and seventy-two, the enumeration of the lay families begins, and the witnesses use this first entry to lay down how the whole list is to be read. The reformed John Gill notes that from here onward the returning captives are described by their families, by the ancestors from whom they sprang or the towns to which they had belonged, and by their numbers, so that of most of them nothing else is now known. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fixes the sense of the recurring word: the children of Parosh are his posterity, all who descended either from Parosh himself or from the family whereof he was the chief, and so, he says, for all the rest.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws a distinction that governs the reading of the entire register. Where the word children is prefixed to the name of a man, as here to Parosh, it means the descendants of that person; but further down, where it stands before the name of a place, it means the inhabitants of that place. The reader is thus to watch whether each head-name is a father or a town, for the list mingles both, some families called after their ancestor and some after the city of their former dwelling.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets Parosh at the head of a long comparison he will pursue name by name, weighing the three authorities against one another. Here at the outset the number agrees in all: Parosh is two thousand a hundred and seventy-two in this register and the same in the parallel roll (Nehemiah 7:8). It is only further on, he observes, that the copies begin to part, sometimes the text here confirmed by the apocryphal Esdras against the larger or smaller figure of Nehemiah, sometimes all three differing, though in ways that seldom matter to the substance. The witnesses thus make of this plain first entry a lesson in method: a genealogy that looks like a bare column of names and figures is in truth a document preserved in three hands, to be read with an eye to its variants and to the difference between a family named from its father and a company named from its town. Parosh, the largest of the lay houses, stands first and sets the pattern for all that follow, the family named from its ancestor and counted at a figure on which, for once, every witness agrees.
4:
The children of Shephatiah, three hundred seventy and two: the second of the lay houses, and one that the witnesses pass over quickly, for its number raises no dispute. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, who set the whole roll of families in parallel columns, list Shephatiah at three hundred and seventy-two and note that the figure stands unchanged in the twin register of Nehemiah 7:9; here the two texts are at one. It is a reminder, they observe, that the many divergences to come are not the rule but the exceptions in a list largely faithful in both its copies.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, comparing the three authorities house by house, reckons Shephatiah among the names where the witnesses do not part company, reserving his closer attention for the entries a little further on, where this register, the roll of Nehemiah, and the apocryphal Esdras begin to differ. The value of such an agreement, small as it seems, is that it fixes the shape of the document: the reader who meets a variation later knows it for a variation, precisely because so many of the surrounding figures, like this one, are steady across the copies.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the larger frame within which even an untroubled number takes its meaning. The catalogue, he insists, survives in three hands that correct one another, and though the sum of the particulars falls short of the grand total, the total itself is sure; each family, whether its figure agrees or diverges, is a real company of returning exiles, named and counted because their return was reckoned worth recording. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had found in the very keeping of such numbers a token of honour, an account written down both as a recompence to those who ventured home and for the benefit of their posterity, that they might know from whom they descended and to whom they were allied. Shephatiah, then, is one of the quiet entries of the list, a house of three hundred and seventy-two souls who came up from Babylon, its number the same in every witness, its ancestor otherwise unknown to us. The witnesses make no more of it than the text does, and their restraint is itself instructive: the register is not a field for invention but a roll to be transmitted faithfully, the plain names and plain numbers of a people whom God had counted worthy to bring home, and whose least house was worth the writing.
5:
The children of Arah, seven hundred seventy and five: and here, at the third house, the register meets its first real divergence from the parallel roll, for where this text reads seven hundred and seventy-five, the twin list of Nehemiah 7:10 gives only six hundred and fifty-two. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley faces the difference squarely and offers the explanation he means to serve for all its like throughout the chapter. Seven hundred and seventy-five, he suggests, marched out of Babylon, but some of them died on the way, others were hindered by sickness or other casualty, so that only six hundred and fifty-two came at last to Jerusalem; the one figure counts those who set out, the other those who arrived. And the like, he says, is to be said of all the similar differences, which it suffices to hint once for all.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the same discrepancy in their parallel columns, Arah at seven hundred and seventy-five here against six hundred and fifty-two in Nehemiah, and take such variations, where they cannot be resolved by Wesley's kind of reasoning, as the ordinary marks of documents copied and recopied by hand. The difference here is among the larger in the whole list, a hundred and twenty-three souls; and yet, they insist, it argues no fault in the record, only the twofold way in which an ancient census might be taken and transmitted. Between a real discrepancy and a mere slip of the pen they do not always decide, content to set the two readings side by side and let the honest divergence stand.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps before the reader the wider reconciliation. The three witnesses to this catalogue, he holds, correct one another, and the surplus of names in the one, added to the other, brings the accounts into agreement; so a figure that seems to contradict its parallel may be, when the whole is reckoned, no contradiction at all. The witnesses thus turn the first stumbling-block of the list into a lesson in patience with an ancient text. Arah's house, whether seven hundred and seventy-five strong at its setting-out or six hundred and fifty-two at its arrival, is a true company of the return; and the gap between the numbers, far from discrediting the record, opens a window on the hardships of the journey home, on the deaths and hindrances of the road, and on the sober fidelity with which the sacred writers preserved even the figures they could not perfectly reconcile.
13:
The children of Adonikam, six hundred sixty and six: a number that has drawn more notice than the obscure name it counts, for the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry cannot pass it without remark. Adonikam, he observes, signifies a high lord, and his children were six hundred sixty-six, just the number of the beast (Rev. 13:18), which is there said to be the number of a man; and he reports that Mr. Hugh Broughton thought the mysterious figure of the Apocalypse had reference to this very man. Henry offers the coincidence for what it is, a curiosity of the sacred arithmetic, one of those small things in a dry list that catch the devout eye.

The grammatical-historical witnesses are more interested in whether the figure is even firm. Keil and Delitzsch, setting the registers in parallel, note that where this text makes Adonikam's house six hundred sixty-six, the roll of Nehemiah 7:18 reads six hundred sixty-seven, a difference of a single soul. Charles Ellicott, weighing the three authorities, finds that here both the parallel roll and the apocryphal Esdras agree in correcting the six hundred sixty-six of this register into six hundred sixty-seven, so that the famous number may itself be a copyist's slip for one just past it.

The witnesses thus hold the verse in a fine balance. On the one side stands Henry's wonder, and Broughton's bolder guess, that the six hundred sixty-six of Adonikam should chime so exactly with the number of the beast; on the other stands the sober textual note that two of the three witnesses read six hundred sixty-seven, and that the striking figure may be no more than an error of transcription. The reader is left to feel both the pull of the coincidence and the check of the criticism, and the witnesses do not force the matter to a decision. What is not in doubt is the house itself: Adonikam, the high lord, whose posterity came up from Babylon some six hundreds strong, one family among the many named and numbered in the roll of the return, its figure remembered chiefly for the accident by which it echoes, whether truly or by a scribe's stray stroke, the darkest number in the book of the Revelation. Keil and Delitzsch would have the reader keep the difference of that single soul steadily in mind, for it is precisely such small variants, gathered and weighed across the three witnesses, that guard the text from both careless trust and careless doubt. Henry's own restraint is the model, who marks the oddity and moves on, neither building doctrine upon it nor quite letting it go.
21:
The children of Bethlehem, an hundred twenty and three: and here the register, having named its families from their ancestors, begins to name them from their towns, so that the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the children of Bethlehem as the inhabitants of that place, the returning remnant of the little city. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way, the poor remnant of Bethlehem's people, and cannot number them without wonder: so little, he exclaims, was Bethlehem among the thousands of Judah, and yet thence must the Messiah arise. The like, he adds, may be said of the two names that follow, Netophah and Anathoth, and of others of the kind, towns whose scattered survivors are here counted home.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers over the same small figure with the same eye to the promise. The children of Bethlehem were but a hundred and twenty-three, he notes, though it was David's city; for Bethlehem was little among the thousands of Judah, yet there must the Messiah be born, as the prophet had said (Micah 5:2). The witnesses find in the meagreness of the number, not a reason for contempt, but the very setting of the wonder, for it is God's way to choose the small and the despised for his greatest works.

So the witnesses turn a bare entry of a hundred and twenty-three souls into a meditation on the humility of the place from which salvation would come. Bethlehem, the city of David and the destined birthplace of David's greater Son, sends home from Babylon only a little band, so few that they are lost among the larger houses of the list; and yet the reader who knows the end of the story sees, in that unregarded name, the town over which the star would one day stand. Clarke and Wesley and Henry converge on the single point: the register, counting the returned inhabitants of Bethlehem, is quietly preserving the place of the promise, keeping a remnant in the city that was little among the thousands of Judah until the fulness of time should come and the Ruler go forth from it whose goings forth had been from of old. Wesley's added word, that the like might be said of Netophah and Anathoth and the rest, keeps the reader from thinking Bethlehem's case unique; yet Bethlehem alone had the promise upon it, and so alone turns its scanty number into a wonder. The smallness of the count, far from diminishing the notice, is the whole of its glory, a hundred and twenty-three names standing guard, as it were, over the cradle that was yet to be.
33:
The children of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, seven hundred twenty and five: three towns counted together, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke identifies them as cities in the tribe of Benjamin, referring the reader to the older notice of their building (1 Chronicles 8:12). These are not the posterity of three men but the returning inhabitants of three places, for by the rule Clarke had laid down at the head of the list, the word children set before the name of a town means those who dwelt in it, the remnant of Benjamite folk coming back to the villages of their fathers.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, pursuing his comparison of the three authorities, marks this entry as one where the text here is confirmed against the parallel roll. Where the register of Nehemiah 7:37 numbers the men of Lod, Hadid, and Ono at seven hundred twenty-one, this text and the apocryphal Esdras agree in reading seven hundred twenty-five, so that the smaller figure of Nehemiah is the odd one out. It is a small divergence, four souls, of the kind Ellicott gathers all through the list, neither hiding it nor magnifying it, but noting on which side the weight of the witnesses falls.

The reformed John Gill keeps before the reader the character of the whole section, that from the head of the roll to its end the captives are described sometimes by the ancestor from whom they sprang and sometimes by the town in which they or their forefathers had formerly dwelt, and that of most of them nothing more is known than what is here set down. Lod and Hadid and Ono belong to the second sort, three Benjamite towns on the western border of the land whose people had been carried away and were now counted home. The witnesses make no legend of them; they fix the places, weigh the number, and let the entry stand as one more company of the return, the men of three villages who came up out of the captivity to dwell again in the cities of their fathers. Clarke's rule, that children set before a town means its inhabitants, keeps the reader from seeking a father named Lod or Ono where none is meant; these are homecomings of townsfolk, not descents from a man, and the seven hundred twenty-five are the returning population of the three places reckoned as one. That so obscure a cluster of names should be preserved at all, and preserved in three witnesses that can be checked one against another, is itself the quiet testimony of the passage, that God kept account of even the least of the houses of his people.
36:
With the priests the register turns from the laity to the ministers of the house, and the reformed John Gill counts them a considerable body: four families only, those of Jedaiah, Immer, Pashur, and Harim, yet numbering together four thousand two hundred and eighty-nine, whom the Jews reckon the heads of the four priestly courses that returned from Babylon. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the transition, that the preceding roll had taken the census of Judah and Benjamin, and now the sacred tribe is told apart.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the proportion and finds it a blessed one. The priests were about a tenth of the whole company, four families making above four thousand two hundred where the whole was above forty-two thousand, so that the tenth was God's part, a blessed decimation. Three of the fathers here named, he observes, were heads of the courses David had appointed (1 Chronicles 24:7); and if Pashur, the fourth, were of the posterity of that Pashur who once abused Jeremiah, it is strange that so bad a man should have a seed so good and so numerous.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott handles the family names with his usual precision. The priests are given by their houses, he notes, their numbers very large in proportion to the other classes; three of the twenty-four courses of the older record are represented, while Pashur, a priestly name not among those twenty-four, appears here beside them. Over the phrase of the house of Jeshua he pauses: it seems to indicate only that the high priest then serving belonged to the race of Jedaiah, who in that case is not the head of the second course in the Chronicles unless he sprang from the high-priestly line of Eleazar. The witnesses thus read the priestly muster both as an honour and as a puzzle. That a tenth of the returning nation should be priests was, to Henry, a token of God's care to furnish his restored house with ministers; that only four of the twenty-four courses came up was, to Gill and Ellicott, a sober fact of the record, the sacred tribe come home diminished but not destroyed. Jedaiah of the house of Jeshua stands first among them, nine hundred and seventy-three strong, the leading priestly family of the return, set at the head of the four houses through whom the altar of the second temple would be served.
37:
The children of Immer, a thousand fifty and two: the second of the four priestly houses, and one the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record in their parallel columns without dispute, for the number of the priests, unlike that of the lay families, stands firm across the witnesses. Immer at a thousand and fifty-two here is a thousand and fifty-two in the roll of Nehemiah 7:40 as well, and so with all four priestly families, whose figures agree in both registers to the sum of four thousand two hundred and eighty-nine.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott had drawn attention to just this feature, that the priests' numbers are large in proportion to the other classes and steady where the lay numbers waver. The agreement is itself a small witness to the care with which the priestly rolls were kept, for the sacred tribe, whose descent had to be proved for the very right to serve, could least afford a slip in its reckoning. Immer, a priestly name known elsewhere in the histories of the return, heads a house of more than a thousand souls, second only to Pashur among the four.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the bare figure into its meaning. That four families of priests should number above four thousand two hundred, a full tenth of the whole company, was to him the tenth that is God's part, a blessed decimation, the restored nation furnished from the first with an abundance of ministers for the house it had come to rebuild. Yet he had noted too the shadow across the muster, that only four of the twenty-four courses returned, so that the priesthood, like the people, came home shrunken from its ancient fulness. Immer's thousand and fifty-two are part of that diminished but sufficient company. The witnesses make of this quiet entry a double lesson: the steadiness of its number, agreeing in every copy, speaks the exactness with which the priestly genealogies were guarded, and the size of its number speaks the goodness of God, who did not leave his altar without servants but brought back, in Immer and his brethren, priests enough to begin again the daily worship at Jerusalem. Nothing more of this Immer is told; his house is remembered only as one of the four through whom the sons of Aaron were restored to their office in the second temple, its thousand and fifty counted faithfully and set down for the honour of the returning ministers of God.
39:
The children of Harim, a thousand and seventeen: the last of the four priestly houses, and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley uses it to untangle a possible confusion. This Harim, he explains, was head of one of the twenty-four courses which David appointed (1 Chronicles 24:8), of all which courses, he observes, not above four or five are found to have returned. And he warns the reader against mistaking him for another of the same name: there is a Harim mentioned earlier in the list, among the lay families, but that Harim was no priest, whereas this one is, as the heading of the priestly section makes plain.

The two Harims, the layman and the priest, are thus as carefully distinguished as the two houses called the children of Elam had been, a reminder that in these registers the same name may serve very different men, and that the class under which a name is set, whether among the people or among the priests, must govern its reading. Wesley's small caution guards the sacred descent, so that a priestly house is not confounded with a lay one that happened to share its founder's name.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keep the wider view. Ellicott had marked that only three or four of the ancient courses were represented among the returning priests, and that their numbers, Harim's thousand and seventeen among them, ran large beside the other classes; Henry had made the whole priestly muster the tenth that is God's part, a blessed decimation, and had mourned that so many of David's courses failed to come up. Harim closes the roll of the four families, and with him the priests are numbered at four thousand two hundred and eighty-nine, a figure the witnesses find agreeing in every copy of the catalogue. The witnesses leave the verse as the seal of the priestly muster: a single house of a thousand and seventeen, carefully marked off from its lay namesake, one of the few courses of Aaron's ancient four-and-twenty that returned to serve the restored altar. That so few of the courses came, yet in such numbers, is the double note of the passage, a priesthood impoverished in its variety but rich in its returning sons, brought home to take up again the ministry of the house of God. The care Wesley takes to keep the priestly Harim apart from the lay one is of a piece with the whole chapter's method, where a name is nothing until its class is known, and where the sacred descent is guarded precisely by such patient distinctions.
40:
The Levites: the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the children of Hodaviah, seventy and four. After the four thousand priests the Levites proper come up a bare seventy-four, and the reformed John Gill marks the smallness of the whole Levitical company, singers and porters included, no more than three hundred and forty-one, where in the days of David they had numbered eight and thirty thousand. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry cannot but wonder at it: taking in the singers and the porters, the Levites did not make three hundred and fifty; time was when they were more forward to their duty than the priests, yet now they lagged, for the wind blows where it lists, and the zeal that marks one house or one age may fail in another.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch account for the tiny number by the make-up of the class. Ellicott notes that the Levites proper, distinct from the priests, fell into two families only, both traced up to one ancestor, Hodaviah, called elsewhere Judah or Hodevah; the hereditary choristers were as few, and of the three great singing-houses of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, only Asaph was represented. Keil and Delitzsch add the textual notes, that the readings Kadmiel and of Hodaviah are the correct ones against the slightly altered forms of the parallel, and that the clause of the children of Hodaviah attaches to Kadmiel, to distinguish him from other Levites of the name.

The witnesses read the meagre seventy-four as a quiet reproach and a quiet providence. The Levites, whose whole office was the service of the house, came home in numbers so small that Henry and Gill alike pause over it, as though the tribe set apart for worship were the slowest to return to the ruined place of worship. Yet the few who came, Jeshua and Kadmiel and their sons of the house of Hodaviah, were enough to begin the work, and the historian counts them with the same care he gives the thousands, for the least company in the service of God is not beneath his notice. The witnesses leave the verse balanced between wonder and thankfulness: wonder that so few of the ministering tribe should answer the call to rebuild, and thankfulness that even these seventy-four came up, a remnant of the Levites to lead again the praises and keep again the courts of the second temple.
41:
The singers: the children of Asaph, an hundred twenty and eight. Of all the temple choirs, only one house returned, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that these were the members of the choir of Asaph, a hundred and twenty-eight strong; the other ancient orders were unrepresented, though the parallel record elsewhere names three, Bakbukiah evidently standing for the order of Heman. The number, they add in their comparison of the registers, is one of those that vary, for where this text reads a hundred and twenty-eight, the roll of Nehemiah 7:44 gives a hundred and forty-eight, a difference of twenty voices.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott had reckoned the choristers among the smallest of the classes, and traced the same fact, that of the three great singing-houses of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun only the sons of Asaph came up. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry folds the singers into his wonder at the whole Levitical remnant, for it was the singers and porters together with the Levites proper that failed to make three hundred and fifty, a poor showing for the tribe whose very calling was the praise of God.

The witnesses find in the single returning choir both a loss and a mercy. That only the house of Asaph should answer the summons, where once three orders had filled the courts with music, was a token of how the service of God had shrunk in the captivity; the harps hung on the willows of Babylon came home fewer than they went. Yet a hundred and twenty-eight singers of Asaph were enough to raise again the temple song, and the historian numbers them, small variation and all, because the praise of the restored house mattered to him as much as its sacrifice. The witnesses do not resolve the twenty-voice difference between the copies, but let it stand as one more of the honest divergences of a hand-copied text, neither the hundred and twenty-eight of this register nor the hundred and forty-eight of its parallel discrediting the other. What they draw out is the thing itself: the sons of Asaph, heirs of the sweet singer's appointed choir, returning to lead the worship of God in a temple not yet rebuilt, the one surviving order of a music that would sound again over the second house as it had over the first. Keil and Delitzsch's further note, that where this text names but the sons of Asaph the fuller record elsewhere reckons three orders, only sharpens the sense of loss and of remnant together, one choir come home to do the work of three.
42:
The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai, in all an hundred thirty and nine. Six families of doorkeepers came up, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that three of the six, the houses of Shallum, Talmon, and Akkub, had dwelt at Jerusalem before the captivity, according to the older record (1 Chronicles 9:17); of the other three, Ater, Hatita, and Shobai, nothing further is known. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott says the same in brief, that the porters, or gatekeepers, number six families, three of which appear in the old Jerusalem.

The number, a hundred and thirty-nine, is one Keil and Delitzsch mark as very near its parallel, for the roll of Nehemiah reads a hundred and thirty-eight, a difference of a single doorkeeper. It is among the least of the divergences that run through the list, so slight that neither Keil and Delitzsch nor Ellicott make anything of it beyond the noting; and yet they note it, for the discipline of the register is to record even the difference of one, that the reader may trust the figures where they agree.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry once more gathers the porters with the singers and the Levites into his reflection on the smallness of the ministering remnant, the whole not reaching three hundred and fifty; and yet he had found even the meanest office of the house an honour, so that the doorkeepers, whose charge was but to keep the gates, are counted with the same reverence as the priests who served the altar. The witnesses read the six little families as the returning wardens of the house of God, come home to take up again their ancient station at its doors. That three of them had kept the gates of Jerusalem before ever the city fell, and now returned to keep them again, gives the notice a quiet continuity, as though the very porters of the first temple were resuming their posts at the threshold of the second. A hundred and thirty-nine men, in six houses, hardly differing from the count of the parallel roll, are set down that the doorkeepers too might have their honour in the record of the return; for it is better, as the psalm has it, to be a doorkeeper in the house of God than to dwell in the tents of wickedness, and these were the men who chose that better place.
43:
The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth. With the Nethinim the register descends to the lowest order of the temple's servants, and the witnesses agree on who they were. The reformed John Gill takes them, with Aben Ezra and Jarchi, for the Gibeonites, given by Joshua to be hewers of wood and drawers of water, or rather for those whom David afterward gave to assist the Levites; the very name Nethinim, he notes, means the given ones. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same, that they were persons devoted to the inferior services of the priests and Levites, commonly supposed the Gibeonites given first by Joshua and again by David when Saul had expelled them (Joshua 9:27).

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch call them temple-bondsmen, and reckon them here with the servants of Solomon, thirty-five families of Nethinim and ten of Solomon's servants, the whole amounting to but three hundred and ninety-two, so that each family can have averaged only eight or nine souls. They note the textual state of the roll: the houses of Akkub, Hagab, and Asnah are wanting in the parallel of Nehemiah, the name Shalmai there appears as Salmai, and one form further on is a combination of two, while the rest of the variations are mere differences of spelling.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the dignity in the lowliness. It is an honour, he says, to belong to God's house, though in the meanest office there; and the Nethinim, with the children of Solomon's servants numbered beside them, are set down among the retainers of the temple as worthy of record as any. The witnesses thus read the opening of this long roll of obscure names as a testimony to the worth of humble service. Ziha and Hasupha and Tabbaoth, whose names would else be wholly forgotten, are kept in the sacred register because they gave themselves to the drudgery of the sanctuary, the wood and the water without which the altar could not burn. That so small a company, in so many little families, should come up at all from Babylon, where nothing bound them but devotion, is itself remarkable; and the historian, counting the given ones with the same care he gives the priests, teaches that in the house of God the lowest place is still a place of honour, and the least servant still a servant of the Most High.
44:
The children of Keros, the children of Siaha, the children of Padon: the roll of the Nethinim runs on through a long file of names that the register gives three to a verse, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch treat the whole file together rather than one by one. These, they explain, are among the thirty-five families of temple-bondsmen who, with the ten houses of Solomon's servants, made up in all but three hundred and ninety-two persons, an average of only eight or nine to a family. The names are proper names of individuals, the founders of the little clans, each prefixed with the children of to mark the household descended from him.

Keil and Delitzsch note that in this stretch the parallel roll of Nehemiah begins to differ. Some houses, they observe, are found here but not there, and here and there a name is spelled otherwise between the two copies, one form in the one register answering to a slightly altered form in the other; yet these variations, they judge, touch only the shape of the words and not the substance of the list. The reformed John Gill keeps before the reader what these given ones were, the descendants of the Gibeonites and of others devoted to the meaner services of the sanctuary, of whom nothing survives but their names in this catalogue.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley had fixed their office once for all, persons set apart to the inferior services of the priests and Levites, and it is in that light the witnesses read even this dry column of Keros and Siaha and Padon. The very obscurity of the names is part of their meaning: these were the humblest of all who served the house, men whose families were so small and so lowly that a whole clan might number but eight or nine, and yet each is written down, household by household, in the roll of the return. The witnesses make no attempt to trace them further, for nothing more can be traced; they are content to preserve them as the text preserves them, a long succession of the given ones coming up from Babylon to resume the drudgery of the temple. That the sacred record should spend so many of its lines on names that carry no story, no number of their own, and no honour but their service, is itself the lesson: in the account God keeps of his house, the doorkeepers and the wood-carriers and the water-drawers are numbered as carefully as the princes and the priests.
49:
The children of Uzza, the children of Paseah, the children of Besai: three more of the Nethinim families, set down in the midst of the long roll of the temple's given ones. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, who number the whole company together, count these among the thirty-five households of Nethinim whose sum, joined with the ten houses of Solomon's servants, came to only three hundred and ninety-two; so small were the clans that each averaged but eight or nine persons, and a name like Uzza or Besai may stand for no more than a single little family come up from Babylon.

The witnesses keep in view the textual care such a list demands. Keil and Delitzsch note that through this part of the roll the parallel register of Nehemiah now agrees and now diverges, a house present in the one and absent in the other, a name spelled here in one fashion and there in another; and they take these differences as the ordinary marks of a document long copied by hand, to be recorded soberly and left to stand. The reformed John Gill keeps the reader mindful of what the whole file of names amounts to, the descendants of the Gibeonites and their fellows, given of old to the service of the sanctuary, of whom nothing now remains but these bare designations in the catalogue of the return.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the sense that redeems the dryness of such a verse. It is an honour, he had said, to belong to God's house, though in the meanest office there; and Uzza and Paseah and Besai, whose names would otherwise have perished utterly, are kept in the sacred roll because they and their fathers had given themselves to the lowly work of the temple. The witnesses read the three obscure houses as a further proof of the same truth the whole roll declares, that God forgets none of his servants, however small their clan or humble their task. These were men bound to Jerusalem by nothing but their office and their devotion, who might have stayed in Babylon unnoticed and unmissed, yet chose to come up and take again the drudgery of the house of God; and the historian, refusing to let even the least of them fall out of the record, numbers them among the given ones, household by household, that their return might be remembered when all else about them was forgotten.
55:
The children of Solomon's servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Peruda. The roll now passes from the Nethinim proper to a kindred class, and the witnesses explain who these servants of Solomon were. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes them, with the Nethinim, for those appointed to the meaner services of the holy house. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is fuller: they are the class mentioned in the history of Solomon (1 Kings 9:21) as formed of the remnant of the Canaanites, a servile order probably inferior to the Nethinim, though generally classed with them, as here in the common enumeration.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds a touch of feeling to the name. These were men who had lived in Solomon's household, and who, after his death, called themselves and their families by that name, esteeming it a great honour that they had been servants to so great a prince. Ellicott presses the honour further into piety: both these classes, he observes, retained through all the captivity their attachment to the service into which they had been received, and, the Levites being now so few, their value in the rebuilding of the temple gave them the special importance they assume in these books.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch complete the reckoning, counting ten houses of Solomon's servants alongside the thirty-five of the Nethinim, the whole together making but three hundred and ninety-two souls. The witnesses read the little company with a certain tenderness. Sprung from a conquered and servile stock, the last of the old Canaanites bound long ago to the drudgery of the sanctuary, they might have been thought least likely to care for Jerusalem; yet they had kept their attachment to the house through all the years of exile, and came up now, when the ministering tribes were thin, to lend their humble labour to the work. Wesley's note that they gloried in the name of Solomon's servants, and Ellicott's that they clung faithfully to their inherited office, meet in a single picture: a class low in birth and low in station, holding fast across the generations to the honour of serving the house of God, and returning, when the day came, to take up that service again. The historian, numbering Sotai and Sophereth and Peruda among the rest, gives even the servants of the servants their place in the roll of the return, that none who loved the sanctuary might go unremembered.
59:
And these were they which went up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsa: the register turns now from those whose descent was clear to a company whose pedigree was in doubt, and the reformed John Gill fixes only the places from which they came, Tel-melah and Tel-harsa and the rest being towns in the land of Babylon where the exiles had dwelt. The men here named could tell the settlements they came out of, but not the fathers' houses from which they sprang.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes this uncertain group the occasion of a searching reflection. There were some, he says, a considerable number, who could not prove themselves Israelites; they presumed they were of the seed of Jacob, but could not produce their pedigrees, and yet would go up to Jerusalem, having an affection to the house and people of God. These, he observes, shamed those true-born Israelites who had lost all relish for the waters of Judah out of which they came (Isaiah 48:1); for here were men with no clear title to the covenant, and yet so drawn to it that they left Babylon to cast in their lot with the returning people.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the company in its place in the document, the families who could not show whether they and their seed were of Israel, named here before the priests whose genealogy could likewise not be found. The witnesses read the verse with a mingled sternness and sympathy. On the one hand the register will not pretend to a descent it cannot verify; these men's Israelite blood remains unproven, and the record says so plainly. On the other hand their very presence in the roll is to their credit, for they came up out of love to the house of God when they might have stayed behind, and the historian does not cast them out but numbers them, only marking that their pedigree failed. Henry draws the lesson home: it is a better thing to be drawn to the people of God without a proof of descent than to be able to prove one's descent and yet care nothing for the covenant. Tel-melah and Tel-harsa, obscure towns of the captivity, send up a company whose faith outran their genealogy, and the witnesses honour them for choosing Jerusalem though they could not name their fathers, a rebuke to every Israelite indeed who had the name and wanted the heart.
60:
The children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda, six hundred fifty and two. Here the register names the doubtful company more nearly, and the reformed John Gill marks the exact nature of their difficulty. Though the immediate parents of these houses were known, Delaiah and Tobiah and Nekoda being named, yet their being set down here shows that they could carry their genealogy no further back, nor make it clearly appear what was the house of their fathers or of what tribe and family they came.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the number, six hundred and fifty-two, and rank these three houses with those who could not prove themselves members of the community of Israel; the parallel roll of Nehemiah 7:62 gives the same company, though its figure differs a little, as so often through the list. The point that troubles the record is not that these men were nobodies, for their nearer fathers were known and named, but that the chain of descent broke off before it reached the patriarchs, so that no man could say for certain they were Israelites.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps up the reflection he had begun, that these families presumed themselves of the seed of Jacob and could not produce their pedigrees, and yet went up to Jerusalem out of affection to the house and people of God. The witnesses find in the six hundred and fifty-two a company neither quite within the covenant people nor willing to be without them. What is not preserved in black and white, Henry had said, will in time be forgotten; and these houses, whose registers had perished somewhere in the long years of exile, stood now unable to prove the very thing they believed of themselves. Yet the historian numbers them, six hundred and fifty-two souls, among the returning host, for their want of a pedigree did not quench their love of Zion. The witnesses read the verse as a sober middle case between the Israelite whose descent was sure and the stranger who had no claim at all: men of broken genealogy, presuming themselves God's people and casting in their lot accordingly, whom the record neither certifies nor rejects, but sets down honestly for what they were, a considerable company come home on the strength of a descent they could believe but not prove. Keil and Delitzsch's placing of the three houses beside the priests who likewise could not be found in the registers shows that the difficulty was not theirs alone; whole strands of the returning people had lost, in the confusion of exile, the papers that would have fixed them in the tribe, and the historian sets down that loss as plainly as he sets down the numbers that survived it.
61:
And of the children of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Koz, the children of Barzillai. From the doubtful laymen the register passes to doubtful priests, three houses that claimed the priesthood but could not prove it. The reformed John Gill notes simply that these could not make out their pedigree, whereas those priests whose descent was clear had been named before. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch name the three, Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, and explain that they could not find their family registers and so were shut out from priestly office; the name Hakkoz, indeed, stands elsewhere as the seventh of the priestly courses, yet the name alone did not suffice, since others bore it too.

The most telling case is the last, and the witnesses dwell on it. Keil and Delitzsch and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott alike tell how a priest had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite, the great man of David's history (2 Samuel 17:27), and had taken her family name, being called after her name, as Ellicott corrects the text, she having probably been an heiress whose inheritance he sought to hold. The house was known ever after by the borrowed name, and with the name it lost the record of its true priestly descent.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the story into a warning. These, he says, gloried in an alliance to an honourable family, and, preferring the dignity of that house to the dignity of the priesthood, would have their children called after Barzillai and their pedigree kept in his register rather than in Aaron's, and so they lost it. In Babylon there was nothing to be got by the priesthood, and therefore they cared not for being akin to it; they had sold their birthright for the honour of being gentlemen, and were justly degraded. Christ, Henry adds, will be ashamed of those that are ashamed of him and his service. The witnesses read the three houses as a solemn instance of a heritage forfeited by neglect. Habaiah and Hakkoz and the sons of Barzillai came up with the returning priests and would gladly now have served at the altar and eaten of its portions; but the proofs they had once thought little worth were gone, and could not be recovered. The lesson the witnesses draw is plain: those who slight their relation to God and his house in the day when it brings no profit may find, when it becomes an honour again, that they have lost the evidence of it beyond recall.
62:
These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found; therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood. The doubtful priests made their search and it failed, and the reformed John Gill explains what they were looking for: the Jews kept public registers of their priests, their descent and marriages and offspring, that it might be known who were fit and who unfit to officiate; and these men sought their names in those rolls and could not find them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the phrase more exactly, that they sought the record of the enregistered, and that being pronounced polluted meant that they were Levitically disqualified, ruled unable to serve.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley enlarges on the diligence with which such registers were kept. The Jews, he says, were generally very exact in their genealogies, from their own choice and interest, that they might preserve the distinctions of the tribes and families, which was needful both to make out their titles to offices and inheritances and to govern their marriages; and from the special providence of God, that so it might be certainly known of what tribe and family the Messiah was born. The failure of these priests to appear in the record was therefore no light matter, but a gap in a chain the whole nation had laboured to keep unbroken.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence to its issue, that the governor forbade them to eat of the most holy things until the question could be divinely resolved. The witnesses read the verse as the strict but merciful working of a jealous order. Strict, because the priesthood could not be entered on presumption; a man who could not prove his descent was, however sincere his claim, put back as one polluted, lest the holy office be profaned by an unproven hand. Merciful, because they were not condemned outright but only suspended, their case left open against a better day. The witnesses feel the pathos of men so near the altar and yet held from it, undone by the loss of a paper; but they feel too the rightness of it, for the honour of the sanctuary hung on the certainty of its ministers, and the very exactness that now excluded these claimants was the same exactness by which, as Wesley says, the tribe and family of the coming Messiah would be surely known. The register that failed them was part of the record that would one day vindicate the Christ.
63:
And the Tirshatha said unto them, that they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim. The excluded priests were suspended by the word of the governor, and the witnesses first ask who this governor was. The reformed John Gill reports that Jarchi understood the Tirshatha to be Nehemiah, but judges with Aben Ezra that the word is rather a title of honour in the Chaldee tongue, a prince or governor, and so takes it here for Zerubbabel, the prince of the returning Jews. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke inclines the other way, that the Tirshatha is generally supposed to be Nehemiah or the commandant of the day, the word being the name of an office; while the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch, with John Wesley, decide firmly for Zerubbabel, the title being interchangeable with Pechah or governor, and probably an old Persian word meaning the feared or reverenced one.

On the ordinance itself the witnesses are agreed. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains that the doubtful point, which no human skill could settle, was referred to divine direction, to be determined when a high priest should arise able to consult God by Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28:30). Clarke and Ellicott note the melancholy fact behind the deferral, that the Urim and Thummim had been lost in the destruction of the city and temple, and, as Ellicott adds, were never restored, so that by them Jehovah was never again inquired of.

The puritan-evangelical reading, which Wesley shares, finds a deeper providence in the loss. The Jews fed themselves with hopes of recovering the ancient oracle, but in vain; and by the want of it they were taught to look beyond it, to expect the great Oracle himself, the Messiah, of whom the Urim and Thummim had been but a type. The witnesses thus make the suspended priests a small window on a large absence. The second temple stood without the oracle by which such a question could be answered, and the governor could only defer the matter to a day that, under that temple, never came. Yet the very emptiness of the place where the Urim had been pointed forward: the people who could no longer ask God by the stones on the breastplate were being schooled to wait for him who would be himself the answer, the priest and the oracle in one. So a ruling about who might eat the holy bread becomes, in the witnesses' hands, a sign of the whole economy's reaching toward Christ.
64:
The whole congregation together was forty and two thousand three hundred and threescore. The register gives its grand total, and at once the witnesses meet the great arithmetical puzzle of the chapter, for the particular sums already listed do not reach it. The reformed John Gill reckons the itemised families, with Zerubbabel and the ten leaders, at but twenty-nine thousand eight hundred and twenty-nine, so that above twelve thousand are wanting; and he answers, with the Jewish chronology, that these were of the other tribes, who joined the return though their particular houses are not named here. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reasons the same way, that the twelve thousand and more not accounted for in the several sums were probably of the tribes besides Judah and Benjamin, Israelites who could not tell their family or city but only that they were of the seed of Jacob.

The grammatical-historical witnesses press the harder fact that the parallel registers themselves differ. Keil and Delitzsch set the three side by side: the total is the same in all, forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty, yet the particulars come in this text to twenty-nine thousand eight hundred and eighteen, in Nehemiah 7:66 to thirty-one thousand and eighty-nine, and in the apocryphal Esdras to yet another figure. These differences, they judge, are owing to mere clerical errors, and attempts to reconcile them otherwise cannot be justified. Charles Ellicott agrees that it is better to suppose errors had crept into the original documents than to force the sums, though he notes that Esdras adds a telling remark, that children under twelve were not reckoned in the count.

So the witnesses divide over the shortfall. Gill, Henry, and John Wesley, with the older expositors, hold that the grand total is right and includes the unnamed thousands of the other ten tribes, whom the particular lists, confined to Judah and Benjamin, left out; Keil and Ellicott hold rather that the total is fixed and true while the itemised sums have suffered in copying, so that the gap is a scribe's fault and not a hidden company. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley allows both, that the twelve thousand five hundred and forty-two added into the total were either of the other tribes or such as were reputed Israelites but could not prove their pedigree. Beneath the dispute the witnesses keep the wonder Henry names, that this returning host, few as it seems, was more than double the number carried captive, a little one become a thousand, and that from so small a seed God would build his people again.
65:
Beside their servants and their maids, of whom there were seven thousand three hundred thirty and seven: and there were among them two hundred singing men and singing women. The reformed John Gill reads the small number of servants as a mark of the returning people's poverty, for these were mostly of the poorer sort, and their bondservants were few, counted apart from the congregation itself. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the same seven thousand three hundred and thirty-seven, and then pause over the two hundred singers, which they find a striking notice. They report, only to reject, the conjecture of Michaelis that the text once read oxen and cows, the Hebrew words resembling those for singing men and women, so that a transcriber might have exchanged the one for the other; the objection, they note, is that the word for cows is nothing like the word for singing-women, and they let the received reading stand.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains why a returning and impoverished company should bring hired musicians at all. The Rabbis, he says, accounted for them as meant to make the return more joyful; but he observes that such singers were hired for lamentation as well as for joy, and thinks they may here have served to supply the lack of Levites, whom the return had brought back so few. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the mournful side, supposing the two hundred were to excite the people's grief, for it had been foretold that they should come weeping (Jeremiah 50:4), with ditties of lamentation over the ruins to which they returned.

The witnesses thus gather several meanings around a single line. The seven thousand servants, few for so great a host, speak the low estate of the exiles, themselves little better than servants, come home with slender retinues; and the two hundred singers, men and women both, speak the mingled mood of the return, at once a homecoming to rejoice in and a coming home to a wasted city to be wept over. Ellicott's note that women too were reckoned among these singers, and Henry's that their office might be grief as much as gladness, meet in the picture of a people whose very music carried both notes. The witnesses leave Michaelis's emendation aside as needless, content that the text means what it says: that among the poor and the few who came up from Babylon there were two hundred trained voices, to raise the song, or the dirge, of a nation returning to its own land and its ruined house.
66:
Their horses were seven hundred thirty and six; their mules, two hundred forty and five. The register turns to the beasts the returning host brought with them, and the reformed John Gill reads the modest count as another token of their poverty: so few horses and mules could carry little more than the goods and baggage, so that the far greater part of the people must have walked home on foot. He notes in passing that some copies of the Latin read six hundred and thirty-six horses, a small variant in a small number.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the beasts of burden together, seven hundred and thirty-six horses, two hundred and forty-five mules, with the camels and asses that follow, and observe that these numbers are identical in the parallel roll of Nehemiah 7:68, though the apocryphal Esdras names the camels first and gives partly different figures, seven thousand and thirty-six horses and five thousand five hundred and twenty-five asses.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws from the same tally a happier reflection. They had gone into captivity, he says, stripped of everything; they now returned from it abounding in substantial riches, seven hundred and thirty-six horses, two hundred and forty-five mules, and, as the next verse adds, camels and asses in their hundreds and thousands, besides gold and silver and rich stuffs. The two readings, Gill's and Clarke's, are not truly at odds but two sides of one truth. Measured against the wealth of a settled nation, the returning company was poor, its riders few and its walkers many; measured against the destitution in which they had entered Babylon, they came home laden, God having blessed them in the land of their captivity with an increase of substance as well as of numbers. The witnesses let the beasts of burden preach this double lesson. The horse and the mule, in the East the mounts of the better sort, were here so few that the notice underlines the humility of the return; yet that a people carried off with nothing should possess them at all, and possess them in the same number their parallel record confirms, was a mark of the mercy that had followed them into exile and was now bringing them, mounted or on foot, back to their own land. Keil and Delitzsch's care to note that the horses and mules stand at the same figures in the parallel roll, where the counts of men so often part, is itself a small reassurance: the very beasts of the caravan were reckoned alike in both witnesses, a token that the inventory of the return was kept with an exactness the discrepancies elsewhere do not overthrow.
67:
Their camels, four hundred thirty and five; their asses, six thousand seven hundred and twenty. The tale of the beasts is completed, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that these numbers, like the horses and mules before them, stand the same in the parallel roll of Nehemiah 7:69, the two registers agreeing exactly in the reckoning of the animals even where they differ in the reckoning of the men. The camels, few and precious, were the beasts for the long desert stages of the journey; the asses, many times their number, were the common carriers of an ordinary household's burdens.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes on that disproportion. The asses, he observes, as throughout the earlier Hebrew history, are the chief and most numerous of the beasts of burden, six thousand seven hundred and twenty of them against a few hundred camels; it is the ass, the patient drudge of the countryside, and not the stately camel, that bears the weight of such a migration. The number tells its own tale of a people not travelling in state but moving house, their goods loaded on the humble beast of the poor.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps up the note he had struck at the horses, that a people who went into captivity stripped of everything now returned abounding in substantial riches, their camels and asses counted in the hundreds and thousands, besides their gold and silver and rich stuffs. The witnesses read the closing line of the inventory as both a plain record and a quiet doxology. Plain, because the historian sets down the camels and asses with the same exactness he gave the priests and the singers, and because their number agrees to a beast with the parallel account, a small proof of the care with which the whole document was kept. A doxology, because the sum of it all, four hundred and thirty-five camels and six thousand seven hundred and twenty asses, added to the horses and mules above, shows a company that God had not sent home empty. The exiles who had hung their harps on the willows returned with beasts enough to carry their substance across the wilderness; and Ellicott's homely observation, that it was the ass above all that bore the load, only deepens the picture of a humble but not destitute people, plodding back to their land behind the patient creatures that had always served the households of Israel.
68:
And some of the chief of the fathers, when they came to the house of the Lord which is at Jerusalem, offered freely for the house of God to set it up in his place. The heads of houses, arriving at the holy site, gave for its rebuilding, and the witnesses are careful about what they found there. The reformed John Gill notes that they came to the place where the temple had formerly stood, and where its ruins still lay; the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott says the same in brief, that they came to the site of the house not yet built, and offered for the building. There was as yet no house, only the ground where it had been and would be again.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the offering itself, that some of the heads of the fathers' houses brought free-will offerings to set the house up in its place, giving after their ability unto the treasure of the work; the verbs, they note, are the very words used of the willing gifts and the rebuilding elsewhere in the sacred history. The gifts were freely given and measured only by what each could bring.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the devotion of the act. They came, he says, to the house of the Lord, though that holy and beautiful house was now a heap of rubbish; yet, like their father Abraham, when the altar was gone they came with reverence to the place of the altar (Genesis 13:4), for it is the mark of Zion's true sons that they favour even the dust of her ruins. And the first house they thought of setting up was the house of God, offering toward it though they had but newly come off a long journey and were beginning the world anew, two costly things. The witnesses read the verse as a portrait of first love in the returning people. They might have built their own dwellings before the Lord's, and spared their purses after the expense of the march; instead the chief fathers, coming to the bare and rubble-strewn site, gave freely toward the temple before they had roofs of their own. Henry's word carries the application: let none complain of the necessary charges of religion, but believe that when the account is balanced they will find it clears the cost. The willing gift at the ruined place of the altar was the seed of the house that would rise there, and the measure of a people who put the honour of God's dwelling before the comfort of their own.
69:
They gave after their ability unto the treasure of the work threescore and one thousand drams of gold, and five thousand pound of silver, and one hundred priests' garments. The witnesses turn to reckon what the freewill offering came to. The reformed John Gill explains that the drams were darics, a Persian coin of gold, worth by one estimate fifteen shillings and by another something more, so that sixty-one thousand of them rose to forty-five or even sixty thousand pounds of English money. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reckons the darics higher still, and the five thousand manehs or minas of silver at some forty-five thousand pounds, making with the gold a sum near a hundred and twenty thousand pounds, besides the hundred garments for the priests; and he sees in it the mercy of God, who in the midst of judgment gave his people favour in the land of their captivity, that they should come home able to give so much. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley cites Bishop Cumberland to the same effect, the gold something more than so many pounds of our money, the silver about thirty-seven thousand pounds sterling.

The grammatical-historical witnesses check the figures against the parallel. Keil and Delitzsch give the darics as worth above sixty-eight thousand pounds and the silver above thirty thousand, but note that the account is more exactly rendered in Nehemiah 7:70. Charles Ellicott is franker still, judging Nehemiah's smaller statement the more correct, and holding that this text's sixty-one thousand is a corruption of forty-one thousand in the gold, and its five thousand pounds of silver and hundred garments but round numbers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the account from the counting-house to the altar. Their offering, he grants, was nothing compared with the offerings of the princes in David's day, who gave by talents (1 Chronicles 29:7) where these gave but by drams; yet these drams, being according to their ability, were as acceptable to God as those talents, like the widow's two mites. The witnesses thus hold together the large sum and the small. Measured by the wealth of the first temple the gift was slender, a returning and impoverished people giving in coins where their fathers had given in talents; measured by their means it was liberal, God having so prospered them in Babylon that, as Clarke says, they came home able to build. And measured by the heart, which Henry makes the true reckoning, it was full, for the freewill offering of the poor, given to their power and beyond it, is weighed in heaven not by its amount but by the love that brings it.
70:
So the priests, and the Levites, and some of the people, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, dwelt in their cities, and all Israel in their cities. The great register closes as it began, with the people settling into their places, and the reformed John Gill notes that the cities were those assigned them out of the several tribes, in which they or their forefathers had dwelt before the captivity. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says the same, that they all went to the cities which had belonged originally to their respective families, each house returning, so far as it could, to its own ancient seat.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears a note of triumph in the phrasing. The emphasis, he says, lies in the closing words, all Israel in their cities; for though Judah and Benjamin had furnished the greatest part of the returning host, this was no partial affair but a national revival, and the constant repetition of in their cities carries that very note. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the harmony of the settlement, that they dwelt in peace, in perfect unity, a blessed presage of their establishment, even as the discords of the state in its latter times would presage its ruin.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a closing reflection. Their cities were out of repair, he grants, yet because they were their cities, such as God had assigned them, they were content to dwell in them, thankful for liberty and property though they had little of pomp or plenty or power. Here was room enough for them all, so that there was no strife among them, but perfect harmony, a good effect of their poverty and a happy presage of their peace. The witnesses read the last verse of the register as the quiet consummation of all that went before. The long roll of names and numbers, families and priests and Levites and given ones, ends not in a heap of statistics but in a people come home, each to his own place, the nation reconstituted city by city upon its old foundations. The unity Henry and Wesley mark, the triumph Ellicott hears in all Israel in their cities, and the humble return to the ancestral towns that Gill and Clarke describe, meet in a single scene of a scattered people gathered again. And Henry turns it to the reader's heart: those who at the call of the gospel renounce sin and return to the Lord shall be guarded through all the perils of the way and arrive safely at the mansions prepared for them in the holy city of God, of which this homecoming from Babylon was but a shadow.
